speaker: Brian Potter
title: Construction Physics Author Brian Potter - Why America Struggles to Build
question: In US highway and urban transit construction, why do relatively small upgrades often drag on for years instead of being completed in weeks?
guest: For roadways specifically, there are a lot of collective action or coordination problems, where there's a very large reluctance to disrupt existing operations in people's lives. People don't want to close down a main road to just rebuild it, even though that would be much faster. So they have to structure things to be as minimally disruptive as possible to existing users of the road. You keep the lanes open and minimize the super disruptive work so it's only on nights, weekends, or certain days, and all that difficulty ends up adding quite a bit of time. You see that in other guises too. For New York subway construction, they famously excavate stations from below instead of coming down from the top using cut and cover, which is often much faster—you just cut open the road, build the station, and rebuild the road. Because people hate disruptive projects, you do it the more expensive, less disruptive way. You also see this in horizontal infrastructure generally, like building a transmission line and having to acquire right of way from all the existing landowners, which slows things down enormously.

points.core: Agencies avoid full road closures to prevent disrupting existing users.
points.note: Accept: reluctance to shut down active roads, keeping lanes open for commuters, minimizing disruption to existing traffic. Do not credit: generic claims about lazy contractors or vague bureaucracy without mentioning avoiding user disruption.

points.core: Restricting disruptive construction work to off-peak hours dramatically extends project timelines.
points.note: Accept: limiting heavy work to nights, weekends, or narrow windows; staging work around live traffic adding duration. Do not credit: generic mentions of bad weather or labor shortages.

points.core: Avoiding street disruption pushes urban transit toward slower underground excavation methods.
points.note: Accept: tunneling/mining stations from below instead of faster cut-and-cover to avoid closing city streets. Do not credit: generic claims that subways are technically hard to build without the cut-and-cover vs. disruption tradeoff.

points.core: Acquiring right-of-way from many individual landowners severely delays horizontal infrastructure.
points.note: Accept: collective action or holdout problems securing easements/land from numerous property owners (e.g., transmission lines, linear corridors). Do not credit: generic mentions of high land prices without multi-owner coordination or right-of-way friction.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Mostly because the actual building is a small slice of the timeline; the rest is process, coordination, and constraints on when crews can work.

Before construction, even modest projects pass through environmental review (NEPA and state equivalents), public comment, design approvals, and funding cycles that depend on multi-year federal and state grant schedules. Litigation, or the threat of it, pushes agencies to over-document everything. Procurement rules then add months: low-bid contracting, bid protests, and the change-order disputes that follow when conditions differ from the plans.

Once work starts, utility relocation is a notorious bottleneck, since buried lines are often poorly mapped and owned by companies with no incentive to move quickly. Work is also staged to keep traffic or trains running, so crews get short night or weekend windows and spend much of each shift setting up and tearing down. Contractors juggle several jobs at once and face weak penalties for delay.

Finally, many agencies have thin in-house engineering staff and rely on consultants, which slows decisions and multiplies handoffs. Researchers such as NYU's Transit Costs Project highlight this last factor in particular.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Relatively small US highway and transit upgrades stretch across years because physical construction is only a fraction of the timeline, and active fieldwork itself is broken into tiny increments. Before work begins, projects must clear environmental reviews, public consultations, right-of-way approvals, and sequential permitting across overlapping local, state, and federal jurisdictions. Rigid low-bid procurement and hollowed-out agency engineering staffs compound delays, turning minor field adjustments into months of formal change-order negotiations, while funding tied to multi-year budget and grant cycles discourages rapid execution. Once on site, US agencies rarely allow full closures to blitz a job. Instead, strict traffic-maintenance mandates and local noise ordinances force contractors to keep lanes and rail lines operating, confining productive labor to brief overnight or weekend windows across dozens of staged micro-phases. Finally, poorly mapped underground water, gas, power, and telecom lines belong to separate public and private utilities with little incentive to hurry, routinely halting the entire site whenever crews uncover an unexpected pipe or cable.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Usually the construction itself isn't what takes years. The process around it is. Before anyone pours concrete, a project has to get through environmental review under NEPA and state laws like California's CEQA. It also needs permits from several agencies and sign-off from utilities, railroads and local governments, whose interests often conflict. Funding comes in pieces through federal grants, state budgets and local matches, and each piece has its own procurement rules, Buy America requirements, and lowest-bid contracting steps. Each step can add months, and the threat of lawsuits pushes agencies to document everything defensively.

On site, moving buried utilities and acquiring property routinely cause delays. Crews also tend to work only at night or on weekends so roads and transit lines stay open, which stretches a few weeks of work across years. Many agencies have cut their in-house engineering staff and rely on consultants, which adds layers of review and change orders. They also tend to avoid risk because they get blamed for failures, not for slowness.

When the rules are suspended, things move much faster. After the 2023 collapse of I-95 in Philadelphia, emergency declarations and round-the-clock work reopened the highway in 12 days.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: In the United States, even minor highway and transit upgrades rarely spend most of their timeline on actual construction; they are stretched out by coordination, permitting, and staging constraints. Projects often cross overlapping municipal, state, and federal jurisdictions, each requiring separate approvals, environmental reviews, and public comment periods before work can begin. Once crews start, underground utilities—water mains, gas lines, and telecom cables owned by private companies—are frequently poorly mapped, forcing work to stall until third-party utility crews relocate them on their own schedules. Agencies also try to minimize daily disruption by keeping roads and rail lines open, which forces contractors to work in cramped, piecemeal stages or brief overnight windows rather than closing a corridor for a rapid rebuild. Finally, patchwork funding streams, strict procurement rules, and low-bid contracts that invite change orders and disputes add further pauses. Combined, these institutional and logistical bottlenecks turn weeks of physical labor into multi-year projects.

A small highway or transit upgrade may take only weeks of hands-on construction, but the project schedule also includes design, funding, permits, bidding, and coordination with utility owners and other agencies. A short stretch of road or a single station can still involve buried utilities, drainage, signals, or accessibility work. If a utility has to move before construction can start, its owner’s schedule can hold up the whole job.

Once construction starts, crews often have to keep lanes open or trains running. They may get only a few hours overnight or on weekends, and each shift can include time to set up barriers or secure the tracks and then reopen them. Work that could be done in one continuous closure may therefore stretch across months. For any given project, the biggest delay might come before crews arrive or from how little time they get on site.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A small upgrade can take years even when the construction itself takes only weeks. The project clock often starts when an agency identifies the need. Before crews can begin, the agency may have to secure funding, finish the design, obtain permits, coordinate with utility owners, and award a contract. Those steps can involve different organizations with different schedules.

Once work starts, keeping a highway or transit line open can stretch a few weeks of labor across months. A transit crew may get only a few hours overnight between the last train and the first, and part of each shift goes to securing the track and making it safe to reopen. A highway crew may have to rebuild one lane at a time to keep traffic moving. An unexpected buried utility can interrupt either job while its owner arranges a relocation.

The physical size of the upgrade is therefore a poor guide to its duration. What often determines the schedule is when crews can get access and which other decisions or jobs must happen first.
